notes: Palme's Social Democrats govern alone (50.1 percent in 1968); template coalition slot 18 holds LO, the party's twin in the labour movement. VPK moved from MD slot 5 to 19 (starting popularity; independent reform communism) and keeps its MD sprite; the Centre Party moved from MD slot 15 to 14 with its MD sprite. KDS (KD sprite) sits in 20 as a Christian moral-protest party, since 14 is taken. Slot 4 is the pro-Moscow Norrbotten wing of VPK, slot 5 the Maoist KFML; slot 7 is the Soviet-aligned peace-front milieu. Slot 10 is the real Tatar-founded Turk-Islam association; other Islamic slots are student/migrant circles.

0.name: Informationsbyrån
0.text:
The Information Bureau is a secret intelligence organisation hidden inside the Defence Staff, formed in 1965 and headed by Birger Elmér. Its existence is unknown to the Riksdag and the public; it answers in practice to the Social Democratic leadership through Defence Minister Sven Andersson, and it recruits informers through the party's network of workplace organisations.

IB registers communists, Maoists and other radicals, infiltrates the Vietnam movement and exchanges intelligence with the CIA, the British services and Israel, despite Sweden's official neutrality. Its leverage lies in its files, its secrecy and its intimate ties to the leadership of the labour movement. In a crisis it would form the core of an authoritarian security regime quietly aligned with the West.

1.name: Moderata samlingspartiet
1.text:
The Moderate Party is the new name adopted in 1969 by the Right Party, Sweden's historic conservative party, in an effort to shed its upper-class image. Led since 1965 by Yngve Holmberg, it won barely 13 percent in the 1968 election, one of its weakest results, and sits in opposition alongside the Centre and Liberal parties without a common programme.

The Moderates defend private enterprise, property rights, lower taxes and a strong national defence, and they attack the growing tax burden and the expanding role of the state. They are the most Western-minded of Sweden's parties, favour close ties to the European Economic Community within the limits of neutrality and distrust Palme's foreign policy. Their base is business, the professions and the wealthier suburbs.

2.name: Folkpartiet
2.text:
The Liberal People's Party, formed in 1934 by the reunion of Sweden's divided liberals, was the main opposition party under Bertil Ohlin in the 1950s. After a heavy defeat in 1968 it chose Gunnar Helén, a cultivated former county governor, as its leader in 1969, hoping to win back the urban middle class from Palme's Social Democrats.

The party stands for social liberalism: a market economy with generous welfare, individual freedom, free trade, development aid and active Swedish engagement in European cooperation. It is the bourgeois party most critical of Social Democratic centralism and tax policy while sharing the commitment to neutrality. Its base is teachers, white-collar workers and the free churches, and its leverage lies in its pivotal position between left and right.

3.name: Sveriges socialdemokratiska arbetareparti
3.text:
The Swedish Social Democratic Party has governed almost without interruption since 1932 and built the Swedish model of the welfare state. In October 1969 Tage Erlander retired after 23 years as Prime Minister and handed party and government to Olof Palme, the 42-year-old former education minister. In the 1968 election the party won 50.1 percent, an absolute majority of the votes.

The party combines full employment, active labour market policy and universal welfare with a mixed economy in which private industry remains dominant. Under Palme it pursues an outspoken foreign policy within armed neutrality, condemning the American war in Vietnam and supporting liberation movements. Its base is the trade-union movement, industrial workers and a growing public sector, and its leverage lies in almost four decades of power.

4.name: Norrbottenskommunisterna
4.text:
The Norrbotten Communists are the pro-Moscow wing of the Left Party – Communists, entrenched in Sweden's far north, where the mines of Kiruna and Malmberget, the Luleå steelworks and the forestry camps have voted communist for generations. Their voice is the Luleå daily Norrskensflamman, and their elder statesman is Hilding Hagberg, party chairman from 1951 to 1964.

They reject Hermansson's 'renewal', defend the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact's intervention in Czechoslovakia, and insist on Leninist discipline and class struggle. They call for sweeping nationalisation, rejection of Western economic integration and close friendship with the socialist countries. Their leverage lies in a solid northern base, the trust of many miners and fraternal ties with the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

5.name: Kommunistiska Förbundet Marxist-Leninisterna
5.text:
The Communist League Marxist-Leninists was founded in 1967 by militants who broke with the Left Party – Communists over its parliamentary reformism and its distance from Peking. The veteran communist Nils Holmberg lends it an old-guard pedigree, but its energy comes from students in Uppsala, Lund and Gothenburg and from its command of the NLF groups that lead street protest against the Vietnam War.

The league upholds Mao Zedong Thought, denounces Soviet social-imperialism and American imperialism alike, and calls for a revolutionary workers' party to overthrow Swedish capitalism. It scorns Palme's anti-war rhetoric as hypocrisy. Its leverage lies in the fervour of its young cadres, its grip on the Vietnam movement and the radical student milieu, and its uncompromising rejection of reformism.

6.name: Nysvenska rörelsen
6.text:
The New Swedish Movement is the creation of Per Engdahl, Sweden's most enduring fascist ideologue, who built it out of his circles of the 1930s and in 1951 helped found the European Social Movement in Malmö as a meeting place for the continent's post-war fascists. Today it is a small community of ageing loyalists and students around Engdahl's publications rather than a party.

The movement preaches a corporate 'New Sweden' beyond parliamentary democracy and class struggle, and a united Europe as a third force between American capitalism and Soviet communism. It despises American mass culture, Western Europe's dependence on Washington and the Social Democratic welfare state alike. Its leverage is intellectual: international contacts, a polished press and its reputation as the respectable face of neo-fascism.

7.name: Stockholmsappellens arvtagare
7.text:
Stockholmsappellens arvtagare is the network of Soviet-aligned peace committees, friendship societies and fellow-travelling intellectuals that grew out of the 1950 Stockholm Appeal, the World Peace Council's petition against nuclear weapons launched in the Swedish capital. Veteran communists, trade-union officials and cultural figures in its ranks travel to the Council's congresses and to Moscow and East Berlin.

The network presents the Soviet Union as the guardian of peace, campaigns for recognition of East Germany and a Nordic nuclear-free zone, and portrays NATO and the United States as the only threat to Swedish neutrality. Its ideal is a Sweden bound by friendship treaties to Moscow and governed by a disciplined left that would silence anti-Soviet agitation. Its leverage lies in embassy contacts, Soviet funding and the pacifist mood of the young.

8.name: Bazargankretsen
8.text:
The Bazargan Circle is a group of devout Iranian students at Swedish universities and technical colleges, most of them future engineers, who reject both the Shah's regime and the Marxism fashionable in the Confederation of Iranian Students. They take their name from Mehdi Bazargan, the engineer and founder of the Freedom Movement of Iran, imprisoned by the Shah's military courts in the 1960s.

The circle seeks a modern, democratic Iran guided by Islamic ethics, constitutional government and independence from foreign powers. It admires the lay thinker Ali Shariati and the reformist cleric Mahmoud Taleghani, and it works with Swedish human rights groups against torture in Iran. Its leverage is limited to student solidarity, contacts with the Freedom Movement's exiles and good relations with Swedish liberals.

9.name: Muharramkommittén
9.text:
The Muharram Committee is a small band of Iraqi and Iranian Shia students in Stockholm and Uppsala who turn the annual mourning for Imam Husayn into political protest. They circulate the rulings and sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965, and the writings of the Iraqi scholar Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, whose followers organise the underground Islamic Dawa Party against the Ba'athist regime in Baghdad.

The committee holds that religious scholars must guide the state and that Muslims owe no loyalty to tyrants such as the Shah. It is hostile to the United States, Israel and atheist communism alike. It has no legal existence and little money; its leverage lies in fervent members and their links to underground clerical networks in Iraq and Iran.

10.name: Turk-Islam Föreningen i Sverige för Religion och Kultur
10.english: Turk-Islamic Association in Sweden for Religion and Culture
10.native_full: Turk-Islam Föreningen i Sverige för Religion och Kultur
10.text:
The Turk-Islamic Association for Religion and Culture was founded in the late 1940s by Tatar and Turkish refugees and immigrants, many of whom reached Sweden from Finland and Estonia, and it is the first Muslim congregation in the country. It has no mosque of its own, but it organises prayers, festivals and burials and is now being joined by Turkish and Yugoslav labour migrants.

The association practises conservative, apolitical Sunni Islam of the Hanafi school and seeks good relations with the Swedish state, the Church of Sweden and the Turkish embassy. It stays well away from Middle Eastern politics. Its leverage lies in its legal standing, its two decades of respectability and its role as the natural partner of Swedish authorities on Muslim affairs.

11.name: Tahrircellen
11.text:
The Tahrir Cell is a handful of Palestinian, Jordanian and Syrian students in Stockholm and Lund who belong to Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. Banned and hunted throughout the Arab world for courting army officers, the party relies on members studying abroad to keep its study circles alive.

The cell rejects nationalism, Ba'athism, Nasserism and every existing Muslim government, demanding a single caliphate that would unite the Muslim world against both Western and Soviet domination. It recruits through intellectual debate rather than violence. In Sweden its leverage is close to nil, but its members return home as trained cadres for the party's underground.

12.name: Brödraskapets studiecirkel
12.text:
The Brotherhood Study Circle meets in rooms rented from Sweden's adult education associations, where Egyptian, Syrian and Iraqi students and a few Turkish workers read Hasan al-Banna, Abul A'la Maududi and Sayyid Qutb, hanged in Cairo in 1966. Its members correspond with Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva and with the exiled Syrian Brotherhood leader Issam al-Attar in Aachen.

The circle calls for an Islamic renewal that is neither capitalist nor communist, for the liberation of Palestine and for Muslims in Europe to build their own mosques, schools and associations. It works through education, charity and patient preaching and respects Swedish law. Its leverage lies in its organisational ambition and in Sweden's generous public support for study circles and voluntary associations.

13.name: Det starka samhället
13.text:
Det starka samhället is Tage Erlander's phrase for the expanding Swedish state, and the name fits the powerful bureaucracy it created. Its core is the National Labour Market Board under Bertil Olsson, which moves workers and subsidises industries across the country, together with the planners of Gunnar Sträng's Finance Ministry and the national boards that run housing, schools and hospitals.

Its technocrats believe that rational planning, not political debate, should allocate labour, capital and housing, and they point to the Million Programme of housing construction and the great school reforms as proof. They are indifferent to bloc politics and impatient with parliamentary delay. Their leverage lies in vast budgets, expertise and the deep habit of Swedes to trust their authorities.

14.name: Centerpartiet
14.text:
The Centre Party, founded in 1913 as the Farmers' League and renamed in 1957, has been transformed under Gunnar Hedlund, its leader since 1949, from a farmers' party into the largest non-socialist party. It won 15.7 percent in 1968, drawing voters from small towns and suburbs anxious about the drain of people from the countryside into the cities.

The party stands for decentralisation, regional balance, family farming and small enterprise, and increasingly for the protection of nature against industrial growth. It firmly supports Swedish neutrality and is sceptical of membership in the European Economic Community. Its leverage lies in its rural organisation, its links to the farmers' cooperative movement and its pivotal role in any future non-socialist government.

15.name: Wallenbergsfären
15.text:
Wallenbergsfären is the industrial empire controlled by the Wallenberg family through Stockholms Enskilda Bank and the holding company Investor, with commanding stakes in ASEA, Atlas Copco, SKF, Ericsson, Saab and Stora Kopparberg. Its patriarch is Marcus Wallenberg, the most powerful private citizen in Sweden, who negotiates directly with Social Democratic prime ministers.

The sphere accepts the welfare state and high wages in return for labour peace, a free hand in industry and policies that favour large export firms. It is internationally minded and quietly Western, linked to American and European capital, while publicly respecting neutrality. Its leverage lies in its ownership of much of Swedish industry, its ability to move investment abroad and its privileged dialogue with the government.

16.name: Svenska Arbetsgivareföreningen
16.text:
The Swedish Employers' Confederation organises private employers in central wage bargaining with the trade unions, a system rooted in the Saltsjöbaden Agreement of 1938. Under its managing director Curt-Steffan Giesecke it is moving from quiet partnership with the labour movement towards a sharper defence of free enterprise against the radical mood in Social Democracy.

SAF argues for market pricing, lower taxes on companies and individuals, managerial authority in the workplace and firm limits on state planning and nationalisation. It funds study centres and publications to persuade Swedes that prosperity comes from enterprise rather than from the state. Its leverage lies in its members' control of jobs and investment and in its role as an indispensable partner in the labour market.

17.name: Svenska Naturskyddsföreningen
17.text:
Founded in 1909, the Swedish Society for Nature Conservation is the country's largest environmental organisation. Public alarm over mercury in fish, DDT in birds of prey and acidified lakes is turning it from a society of naturalists into a campaigning movement, while Sweden prepares to host the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm.

The society calls for strict controls on pollution and pesticides, protection of the last wild rivers of Norrland from hydroelectric dams and limits on the exploitation of forests and coasts. Its youth wing, Fältbiologerna, is drifting towards direct action and a critique of growth itself. Its leverage lies in scientific credibility, a broad membership and the growing environmental conscience of Swedish politics.

18.name: Landsorganisationen i Sverige
18.text:
The Swedish Trade Union Confederation unites some 1.6 million blue-collar workers and forms, with the Social Democratic Party, one of the two arms of the Swedish labour movement. Arne Geijer has led it since 1956, and its economists Gösta Rehn and Rudolf Meidner designed the solidaristic wage policy at the heart of the Swedish model. A wildcat strike by the LKAB miners in Kiruna, begun in December 1969, now challenges its centralised authority.

LO seeks equal pay for equal work, full employment, industrial democracy and a greater share of economic power for workers. It supports neutrality and solidarity with the Third World, and its left grows impatient with private ownership. Its leverage lies in its membership, its funds and its decisive voice within the governing party.

19.name: Vänsterpartiet kommunisterna
19.text:
The Left Party – Communists is the former Communist Party of Sweden, renamed in 1967 under Carl-Henrik Hermansson, who has led it since 1964 and turned it towards a democratic, independent socialism. It condemned the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, yet the crisis still cost it dearly, and it won only 3 percent and three seats in the election that autumn.

The party seeks a socialist Sweden built through parliamentary democracy, public ownership of the banks and key industries, and strict neutrality outside both blocs. It is close to the New Left on Vietnam, the environment and the Third World, but faces a pro-Soviet minority in Norrbotten and Maoist breakaways on campus. Its leverage lies in parliamentary arithmetic and its standing among radical workers and intellectuals.

20.name: Kristen Demokratisk Samling
20.text:
Christian Democratic Unity was founded in 1964 as a protest movement after more than two million Swedes signed a petition against cutting Christian instruction in schools. Led by Birger Ekstedt and backed by the Pentecostal leader Lewi Pethrus, it won 1.5 percent in 1968, too little for a seat in the Riksdag.

The party mobilises believers against what it sees as the moral collapse of the permissive society: pornography, liberal abortion, the decline of the family and the secular arrogance of the Social Democratic establishment. It speaks for the free churches and the countryside against Stockholm's cultural elite. Its leverage lies in a devoted core of church members and in a reservoir of protest against secularisation that the major parties ignore.

21.name: Nordiska Rikspartiet
21.text:
The Nordic Reich Party was founded in 1956 by Göran Assar Oredsson, a veteran of Sweden's small post-war National Socialist groups, and he leads it together with his wife Vera. It is Sweden's most openly neo-Nazi organisation: small but noisy, it holds uniformed meetings, spreads propaganda in schools and on the streets and clashes with left-wing activists.

The party venerates Adolf Hitler, preaches Nordic racial unity and anti-Semitism and calls for a Greater Nordic Reich purged of communists, Jews and immigrants. It rejects both American liberalism and Soviet communism. Its leverage is minimal, resting on a few hundred activists, international neo-Nazi contacts and the publicity its provocations attract.

22.name: Försvarsmakten
22.text:
The Swedish Armed Forces maintain one of the strongest militaries in Europe to back the policy of armed neutrality: a conscript army able to mobilise some 800,000 men, a navy built for the Baltic and an air force flying home-built Saab Draken fighters, with the new Viggen about to enter service. The Supreme Commander, General Torsten Rapp, answers to Defence Minister Sven Andersson.

The officer corps is loyal to the Crown and the constitution and quietly expects Western help if the Soviet Union attacks, a secret shared with few politicians. Its leaders regret the abandonment of Swedish nuclear weapons plans and resent the radical youth's contempt for the military. Their leverage lies in conscription, the defence industry and the prestige of total defence.

23.name: Huset Bernadotte
23.text:
The House of Bernadotte has reigned since 1818, when the French marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte became King Karl XIV Johan. King Gustaf VI Adolf, a respected archaeologist, has reigned since 1950 and turns 88 this year; his heir is his grandson, Crown Prince Carl Gustaf, born in 1946, whose father died in an air crash in 1947.

The monarchy is popular but politically weak, and the Social Democratic programme still calls for a republic. Constitutional reform now under discussion is expected to strip the Crown of its remaining formal powers. The royal house stands for continuity, national unity and Sweden's dignity abroad. Its leverage lies in personal popularity and the loyalty of the officer corps and the conservative parties.
